thread.title_full: Kennewick unveils 1st look for city hall's proposed $35M renovation - NewsBreak

author: Eric Rosane
title: Kennewick unveils 1st look for city hall's proposed $35M renovation - NewsBreak
text:
By Eric Rosane ,
8 hours ago Kennewick council members are still deciding what they want a new city hall to look like. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com The Kennewick City Council and community members got an early look Tuesday night at what a new city hall could look like.
Contractor Architects West delivered their final presentation to the city after eight months of work to design, plan and price replacement concepts. That also included an assessment of the bones of Kennewick’s 60-year-old city hall at 210 W. 6th Ave.
The presentation included early computer-generated renderings of what the interior and exterior could look like.
Current details include a 60 to 70 foot setback from entrance with a courtyard, an amphitheater on the north face, a one-stop service center, a squircle-shaped council chambers with a skylight, reception desk area, offices and meeting rooms.
A final report will be delivered in the coming weeks, and a decision on specifics is expected at the council’s Aug. 18 meeting. After that, Kennewick will seek bids on the 18-month design process and an 18-month build.
The Kennewick City Hall building at 210 W. Sixth Ave. in downtown Kennewick. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com “I think the most important thing to recognize is we have to do something,” Mayor Jason McShane told the Tri-City Herald. “The existing facility needs major repairs. Roofing damage and things like that have to be resolved. So, we have to make a decision and these decisions are hard to make.”
Plans to build new $35M city hall The council wants to demolish the building and replace it at the current site with a new two-story, 46,000-square-foot building that would cost about $520 to $620 per square foot. The final price tag could range from $29 million to $35.5 million.
The city does not plan to raise taxes to cover the cost of the new construction.
It would instead be paid for upfront with a 20-year limited tax obligation bond sale and repaid with existing revenue. The debt will be repaid with 4.5% interest and require an annual servicing of $2.7 million, according to previous Herald reporting .
A computer-generated rendering of the proposed Kennewick City Hall. The new facility would last at least 75 years and allow room for the city to grow. The concepts for a civic master plan showed a new aquatics facility could replace a baseball field and be built north of city hall, near the Mid-Columbia Library’s Keewaydin branch.
Earlier design options toyed with the concept of demolishing and accommodating the Museum at Keewaydin in a new city hall, but Tuesday night’s designs showed the building still standing.
A computer-generated rendering of the proposed Kennewick City Hall. Misty Ayers, the museum’s administrator, said she is in support of a plan that retains the current 40-year-old museum with its priceless artifacts.
She added that she hopes several outdoor displays will be preserved, and she has issue with changes to their street and parking, questioning the feasibility of an amphitheater between city hall and the museum.
“Overall, I like this plan that keeps the museum and our access to the basement. I hope the Museum at Keewaydin will remain open to families, travelers and classrooms for many decades to come,” Ayers said.
“Nowhere else in Kennewick can you learn of our city’s history — not just read about it, but view items pioneers used and imagine their experiences, sit at a desk that was once in a 1905 one-room schoolhouse, see an arrowhead that may have been used to hunt a Columbian Mammoth 12,000 years ago,” she continued.
City officials and designers have cautioned that these designs are early in concept and that meetings with stakeholders on programming and design elements will take place in future months.
A site plan shows the campus layout of Kennewick’s new city hall, which will be rebuilt at 210 W. 6th Ave. Courtesy City of Kennewick/Architects West Costs unveiled for moving staff The cost to relocate 75 city hall employees to temporary work spaces and offices during the nearly two -year construction process could cost upwards of $400,000.
That includes about $250,000 for three modular offices and a data service relocation estimate of about $150,000. It does not include any additional moving costs, or any savings that could be made by temporarily using empty city-owned facilities, such as the former fire station at 600 S. Auburn Street.
A computer-generated rendering of the proposed Kennewick City Hall. “I think we’ve got a pretty good plan where we can kind of spread some people out. But we also have a few options for some smaller office space within this downtown core that we could utilize as well,” said City Manager Erin Erdman.
The city also received a total cost estimate for an option to renovate instead of rebuild city hall, which would prolong the life of the leaky and decrepit 39,000-square-foot building.
That would cost $23 million to $26 million, with an average square footage cost of between $460 and $530. On the high end, a new build is only about 17% more expensive per square foot.
A computer-generated rendering of the proposed Kennewick City Hall. Principal architect Marcus Valentine cautioned against comparing the two proposals because they would be substantially different projects.
“The cost per square foot doesn’t just buy the exact same space in either case,” he said. “There is more bang for the buck with the new construction cost. Even though that cost per foot is higher, that money has a greater return and a longer return for the city in the way that the systems can be designed, the way the spaces can be designed over the life of the building.”
A computer-generated rendering of the proposed Kennewick City Hall. Still, the council appears poised to move forward with the demolition-and-build plan when it meets next month, but there remains some hesitation.
Councilman Brad Klippert said he’s still weighing his options on which choice to support. He said he’s price conscious, and says he wants to make the right decision for the taxpayers. He’s leaned toward the cheaper renovation option, and urged designers last month to come back with the cost estimates.
McShane has been adamant about drafting a formal civic campus master plan, and said this week’s presentation was a “step in the right direction” for that effort. He said the council has now come into understanding of the true scope of the project, and is ready to take the next step forward.
“This is the beginning of a process, not the end,” he said. “This is the final presentation on the study that really kicks off the public involvement that we saw.”

Current details include a 60 to 70 foot setback from entrance with a courtyard, an amphitheater on the north face, a one-stop service center, a squircle-shaped council chambers with a skylight, reception desk area, offices and meeting rooms. The concepts for a civic master plan showed a new aquatics facility could replace a baseball field and be built north of city hall, near the Mid-Columbia Library’s Keewaydin branch.
